entry.title: Ruby Versions and Gems
entry.content:
rbenv is a lightweight Ruby version manager for Unix-like systems, which dynamically intercepts Ruby executable commands using shims, switching versions by checking the RBENV_VERSION environment variable, searching per-project .ruby-version file, or falling back to the global ~/.rbenv/version file.

# install rbenv (Linux/macOS)
curl -fsSL https://rbenv.org/install.sh | bash
rbenv help                  # man rbenv: view help text for any rbenv command

rbenv install -l            # list latest stable versions for each Ruby
rbenv install <version>     # install a Ruby version:

rbenv versions              # list all locally installed Ruby versions known to rbenv
rbenv version               # view the currently active Ruby version

rbenv shell <version>       # set a shell-specific Ruby version
rbenv local <version>       # set a directory-specific Ruby version
rbenv global <version>      # set the global Ruby version

rbenv which <command>       # view the executable path that a command resolves to

RubyGems is the official package management framework for the Ruby programming language.

  • A gem is a standardized package containing a Ruby library or program, which includes metadata (such as a name, version, and platform), the executable code, documentation, and a .gemspec file.

  • The gem command-line tool can be used to discover, install, update, and manage these packages.

    gem help                # view help text for any gem command

gem search <REGEXP>     # seach remote gems whose name matches the regexp

gem install <GEMNAME>   # install local or remote gem into a gem repository
gem uninstall <GEMNAME> # remove an installed gem

gem list <REGEXP>       # list installed Gems

  • The bundle is the command-line tool provided by the Bundler gem, which is designed to manage a project’s dependency.

    bundle help  # view help text for each subcommand

gem install bundler      # install the latest Bundler
bundle update --bundler  # update the recorded version in `Gemfile.lock`

bundle install  # install the gems specified by the Gemfile or Gemfile.lock
bundle update   # update dependencies to their latest versions
bundle lock     # create / update a lockfile without installing

bundle list     # list all the gems in the bundle
bundle outdated # list installed gems with newer versions available

bundle exec     # execute a script in the current bundle

bundle show     # show the source location of a particular gem in the bundle
bundle info     # show information for the given gem in your bundle

bundle platform # displays platform compatibility information

bundle config   # specify and read configuration options for Bundler

bundle doctor   # check the bundle for common problems
    Bundler is a default gem, so every Ruby installation always contains a version of it that cannot be uninstalled. Installing a newer version does not replace the default one. Both stay available.

    Bundler supports overriding gem sources with mirrors to configure rubygems.org as the gem source in Gemfile while still using mirror to fetch gems.

    bundle config set --global mirror.SOURCE_URL MIRROR_URL

    For example, to globally mirror https://rubygems.org to an alternate public endpoint:

    bundle config set --global mirror.https://rubygems.org https://example.org

    Alternatively, to configure a mirror only for a project using a regional service:

    bundle config set --local mirror.https://rubygems.org https://mirrors.tuna.tsinghua.edu.cn/rubygems/

    Enable deployment mode in CI or on a deployment host so Bundler installs gems under vendor/bundle and refuses to change an out-of-date Gemfile.lock:

    bundle config set --local deployment true

    BUNDLE_DEPLOYMENT is equivalent to enabling BUNDLE_FROZEN and setting the installation path to vendor/bundle. BUNDLE_FROZEN prevents Bundler from making automatic changes to Gemfile.lock, so the lockfile must be committed and kept in sync with the Gemfile.

    Enable lockfile checksums to record the expected checksum of each gem and reject a package whose contents differ from the recorded value:

    bundle config set --local lockfile_checksums true
bundle lock --add-checksums  # add checksums to an existing lockfile

    Some mirrors may publish incomplete or stale checksum metadata. If a mirror leaves checksum values absent, generate or refresh the lockfile using a mirror with complete metadata or the official source, then commit it; deployments can still download the gems from the mirror and verify them against the recorded checksums. Missing checksums are also expected for Git and path dependencies.

    The settings are stored in .bundle/config; keep that file machine-specific and commit Gemfile.lock instead.

  • A Gemfile is a file that describes an application’s gem environment for Bundler, which is evaluated as Ruby code, in a context which makes available a number of methods used to describe the gem requirements.

    A Gemfile.lock is the output of dependency resolution, recording the exact version of every gem, direct or transitive.
entry.summary: A practical reference for managing Ruby versions and project dependencies with rbenv, RubyGems, and Bundler.

entry.title: TeX and LaTeX: Mathematics and Typesetting

link.title: TeX and LaTeX: Mathematics and Typesetting

entry.content:
TeX is a text formatting and markup language developed by D. Knuth in the late 1970s and early 1980s, which has become the de facto standard for document preparation in mathematics and certain areas of the physical sciences because of its unsurpassed utility in typesetting mathematical formulae. LaTeX is an extension of TeX, which for purposes of discussion can be thought of as a third-party macro package for TeX to provide a logical system for document preparation, where the author does not have to give specific formatting instructions in order to achieve a particular look; the look is provided by an external document class description. [1] [2]

TeX is named after the Greek letters tau (τ), epsilon (ε), and chi (χ), reflecting the word τέχνη (téchnē), meaning "art," "craft," or "skill" in Greek. It is pronounced "tech" (as in technology), not "teks." LaTeX stands for Lamport TeX, named after its creator, Leslie Lamport. It is pronounced "LAY-tech" or "LAH-tech."

TeX Live is one of the major TeX systems (e.g., MiKTeX and TeX Live) that provides binaries for most flavors of Unix, including GNU/Linux and macOS, and also Windows. It includes the major TeX-related programs, macro packages, and fonts that are free software, including support for many languages around the world. Many Unix/GNU/Linux operating systems provide TeX Live through their own distributions and package managers. TeX Live is supported by the TeX Users Group and many other user groups around the world. [3 ]

MathJax is an open-source JavaScript display engine for LaTeX, MathML, and AsciiMath notation that works in modern browsers, with built-in support for assistive technology such as screen readers, including automatic speech generation and an expression explorer that can be used to investigate typeset mathematics at a more granular level than the complete expression. [4]

TeXLive.net is a powerful online site to edit TeX snippets, run LaTeX, and display PDF documents or error logs.
  • 1. Mathematics
    • 1.1. Rules
    • 1.2. Superscripts and subscripts
    • 1.3. Fractions and binomials
    • 1.4. Greek letters
    • 1.5. Mathematical operators and symbols

  • 2. STEM in Asciidoctor

  • Bibliography

1. Mathematics

LaTeX allows two writing modes for mathematical expressions: the inline math mode and display math mode: [5]

  • inline math mode is used to write formulas that are part of a paragraph:

    The Pythagorean theorem is \(a^2 + b^2 = c^2\).

    The Pythagorean theorem is \(a^2 + b^2 = c^2\).

  • display math mode is used to write expressions that are not part of a paragraph, and are therefore put on separate lines

    The quadratic formula is:

\[
x=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}
\]

    The quadratic formula is:

    \[ x=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a} \]

2. STEM in Asciidoctor

Asciidoctor supports mathematical notation through STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics) processing. It supports both AsciiMath and LaTeX-style mathematical expressions. When generating HTML, Asciidoctor can prepare STEM expressions for rendering by a JavaScript-based mathematics engine such as MathJax. [6]

2.1. Enabling STEM support

A document-level attribute can override the global setting when necessary.

To enable STEM processing, set the stem attribute in the document header or configure the stem attribute globally in the site’s _config.yml file for using the Jekyll Asciidoc plugin:

asciidoctor:
  attributes:
    stem: latexmath

The value latexmath selects LaTeX syntax as the default for STEM expressions. If no notation is specified, Asciidoctor defaults to AsciiMath.

2.2. Rendering mathematics with MathJax

Asciidoctor processes STEM macros during document conversion, but HTML output generally requires a mathematics renderer to display the expressions as formatted mathematics in the browser. MathJax is a JavaScript library that can render LaTeX mathematics in HTML.

<script>
  window.MathJax = { (1)
    options: {
      ignoreHtmlClass: 'nostem|nolatexmath' (2)
    },
    tex: {
      inlineMath: [['\\(', '\\)']], (3)
      displayMath: [['\\[', '\\]']], (4)
      tags: 'none' (5)
    },
  };
</script>
<script defer
    src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/mathjax/4.1.3/tex-chtml.min.js" (6)
    integrity="sha512-kO24RkUwCpSCXtdV9p2FM/5isVLi06qQPGlE+AsOx8kN9MTc6Mk7qlZBSEh/b7bvCr2vEWlZLAdp20QLkB/qPg=="
    crossorigin="anonymous"
    referrerpolicy="no-referrer">
</script>
1 Defines the MathJax configuration before the library loads.
2 Excludes HTML elements whose class matches nostem or nolatexmath from MathJax processing.
3 Sets \(…​\) as the delimiters for inline mathematics.
4 Sets \[…​\] as the delimiters for display mathematics.
5 Disables automatic equation numbering.
6 Loads the MathJax TeX-to-Common-HTML component. The tex-chtml.min.js filename indicates TeX input processing, Common HTML output, and a minified JavaScript file.

2.3. STEM macros versus MathJax delimiters

There are two main ways to include mathematical expressions in an AsciiDoc document: using Asciidoctor’s STEM macros or writing LaTeX expressions directly between delimiters recognized by MathJax.

Method Example Processing

STEM macro

stem:[y = mx + c]

Asciidoctor recognizes the macro and processes the expression according to the configured STEM notation.

Explicit LaTeX macro

latexmath:[\frac{a}{b}]

Asciidoctor recognizes the macro and interprets its content as LaTeX notation.

Raw MathJax delimiters

\( \frac{a}{b} \)

MathJax processes the delimiters in the generated HTML, provided they are preserved and recognized by its configuration.

The distinction matters because Asciidoctor processes STEM macros during document conversion, whereas MathJax normally renders mathematical expressions in the browser after the HTML has been generated. The two approaches can coexist, but their processing pipelines should be configured consistently.

For a Jekyll site using Asciidoctor, prefer stem:[...] for inline mathematics and [stem] blocks for display mathematics to make the source more explicit and avoid relying on MathJax to recognize raw delimiters throughout the generated HTML.

  • Use the stem inline macro to include a mathematical expression within a paragraph:

    The equation of a straight line is stem:[y = mx + c].

    The equation of a straight line is \(y = mx + c\).

    To specify LaTeX notation explicitly, use the latexmath macro:

    The quadratic equation is latexmath:[ax^2 + bx + c = 0].

    The square brackets delimit the macro’s content. Unlike raw MathJax delimiters, the Asciidoctor STEM macro does not require wrapping the expression in \(...\) or $...$.

  • For a standalone equation, use a delimited STEM block:

    [stem]
++++
x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}
++++

    Because the document header specifies :stem: latexmath, the expression is interpreted as LaTeX and rendered as a display equation:

    \[x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}\]

    Alternatively, explicitly specify the notation (e.g., LaTeX) on the block:

    [latexmath]
++++
\int_0^1 x^2\,dx = \frac{1}{3}
++++

Bibliography

  • [2] https://info.arxiv.org/help/tex.html

  • [3 ] https://tug.org/texlive/

  • [4] https://www.mathjax.org/

  • [5] https://www.overleaf.com/learn/latex/Mathematics

  • [6] https://docs.asciidoctor.org/asciidoc/latest/stem/

  • [7] https://docs.asciidoctor.org/asciidoctor/latest/stem/mathjax/

TeX is a text formatting and markup language developed by D. Knuth in the late 1970s and early 1980s, which has become the de facto standard for document preparation in mathematics and certain areas of the physical sciences because of its unsurpassed utility in typesetting mathematical formulae. LaTeX is an extension of TeX, which for purposes of discussion can be thought of as a third-party macro package for TeX to provide a logical system for document preparation, where the author does not have to give specific formatting instructions in order to achieve a particular look; the look is provided by an external document class description. [1] [2] TeX is named after the Greek letters tau (τ), epsilon (ε), and chi (χ), reflecting the word τέχνη (téchnē), meaning "art," "craft," or "skill" in Greek. It is pronounced "tech" (as in technology), not "teks." LaTeX stands for Lamport TeX, named after its creator, Leslie Lamport. It is pronounced "LAY-tech" or "LAH-tech." TeX Live is one of the major TeX systems (e.g., MiKTeX and TeX Live) that provides binaries for most flavors of Unix, including GNU/Linux and macOS, and also Windows. It includes the major TeX-related programs, macro packages, and fonts that are free software, including support for many languages around the world. Many Unix/GNU/Linux operating systems provide TeX Live through their own distributions and package managers. TeX Live is supported by the TeX Users Group and many other user groups around the world. [3 ] MathJax is an open-source JavaScript display engine for LaTeX, MathML, and AsciiMath notation that works in modern browsers, with built-in support for assistive technology such as screen readers, including automatic speech generation and an expression explorer that can be used to investigate typeset mathematics at a more granular level than the complete expression. [4] TeXLive.net is a powerful online site to edit TeX snippets, run LaTeX, and display PDF documents or error logs. 1. Mathematics 1.1. Rules 1.2. Superscripts and subscripts 1.3. Fractions and binomials 1.4. Greek letters 1.5. Mathematical operators and symbols 1.6. Summations, products, and integrals 1.7. Brackets and parentheses 1.8. Matrices and equations 1.9. Functions and named operators 2. STEM in Asciidoctor 2.1. Enabling STEM support 2.2. Rendering mathematics with MathJax 2.3. STEM macros versus MathJax delimiters Bibliography 1. Mathematics LaTeX allows two writing modes for mathematical expressions: the inline math mode and display math mode: [5] inline math mode is used to write formulas that are part of a paragraph: The Pythagorean theorem is \(a^2 + b^2 = c^2\).
