7.2.3. Inmon, Kimball, and Data Vault

Data modeling for data lakes and warehouses is the process of transforming raw data from its various forms, such as structured and semistructured, into a structured model of rows and columns using distinct approaches like the Kimball, Inmon, and Data Vault methodologies.

A wide table is a highly denormalized table with a very wide collection of fields, used in a relaxed data modeling approach within a columnar database that has a defined schema, unlike a NoSQL wide column store, which allows a flexible schema where columns can vary by row.

  • The Inmon model, developed in 1989 by Bill Inmon, the father of the data warehouse, physically separates the source system from the analytical system to prevent bogging down production transactional databases with long-running queries.

    • The Inmon model requires a subject-oriented focus, integrating all details for a specific area into a highly normalized structure that is both nonvolatile and time-variant to enable historical queries in support of management’s decisions, positioning the warehouse strictly for analytics, not OLTP.

    • In the Inmon model, ETL is used to integrate data into a central, highly normalized (3NF) data warehouse, with strict normalization minimizing data redundancy to create a single source of truth that then feeds denormalized data marts for analysis.

      • While a data warehouse serves as an enterprise-wide, highly normalized single source of truth for granular data, a data mart is a smaller, often denormalized, departmental subset derived from it for specific analytical purposes.

      • For instance, in an ecommerce scenario, data from source systems is ETLed into the 3NF data warehouse, from which it is further transformed and placed into department-specific data marts (commonly star schemas) to facilitate tailored reporting and analysis.

  • The Kimball model, developed by Ralph Kimball in the early 1990s, is a data modeling approach that contrasts with the Inmon method by emphasizing denormalization and a bottom-up design where the data mart effectively becomes the data warehouse.

    • In the Kimball approach, data is modeled using fact tables (quantitative data) and dimension tables (qualitative data), with dimension tables surrounding a single fact table to form a star schema, much like planets orbiting a central sun.

      A snowflake schema is a special case of the star schema, where the key difference is that star schemas use denormalized, single-table dimensions for fewer joins and faster queries, while snowflake schemas normalize dimensions into multiple related tables, leading to more joins and potentially slower queries but with reduced data redundancy.

      • A fact table is the first type of table in a star schema that includes immutable, append-only factual, quantitative, and event-related data, typically narrow and long with few columns but many rows that represent events.

        • Each row represents the lowest possible grain of data while aggregations or derivations are performed in a downstream query, data mart table or view.

        • A fact table is not designed to reference other fact tables, while it exclusively references dimension tables.

        • A fact table features numerical data types (integers and floats) with no strings, and keys that reference dimension tables for their respective attributes.

      • A dimension table is the secondary type of table in a star schema that provides reference data, attributes, and relational context for fact table events, which is typically wide and short, denormalized, and describes events' "what, where, and when."

  • The Data Vault is an agile and scalable data modeling methodology created by Dan Linstedt as an alternative to the Kimball and Inmon approaches that separates structural data from attributes by loading data directly from source systems into an append-only model composed of hubs for business keys, links for relationships, and satellites for attributes.

7.3. Transformations

Data transformation unifies and integrates data, enhancing its value by manipulating, saving, and persisting results for downstream use. Unlike queries that retrieve data, transformations store results, making complex data pipelines more manageable and cost-effective by avoiding repeated, resource-intensive computations. Orchestration is crucial for combining these discrete transformation operations across various systems.

7.3.1. Batch Transformations

Batch transformations process data in discrete chunks on a fixed schedule, supporting ongoing reporting, analytics, and machine learning models, in contrast to continuous streaming transformations.

7.3.1.1. Distributed Joins

Distributed joins break down logical joins into smaller node joins across a cluster, often using broadcast joins when one side of the data is small enough to fit on a single node, or more resource-intensive shuffle hash joins that redistribute data across nodes otherwise.

  • A broadcast join is an asymmetric distributed join where a small table, capable of fitting on a single node, is sent to all nodes to be joined with parts of a larger, distributed table, resulting in a less compute-intensive and more performant operation, often enabled by prefiltering and query optimization.

    In practice, join reordering optimizes query performance by applying filters early and moving smaller tables to the left (for left joins), which dramatically reduces the amount of data processed and enables broadcast joins for improved performance and reduced resource consumption.
    Figure 1. In a broadcast join, the query engine sends table A out to all nodes in the cluster to be joined with the various parts of table B

  • A shuffle hash join is a symmetric distributed join where both large tables, incapable of fitting on a single node, are repartitioned and shuffled across the network by the join key using a hashing scheme, resulting in a more resource-intensive and less performant operation, often necessary when a broadcast join is not feasible.

    A hashing scheme is a function that maps a data record’s join key to a specific node, ensuring all records with the same key are sent to that node for local joining.
    Figure 2. In a shuffle hash join, tables A and B are initially distributed across nodes, then repartitioned by a join key using a hashing scheme, reshuffled to specific nodes, and finally joined locally on those nodes.
7.3.1.2. ETL, ELT, and data pipelines

Traditional ETL (Extract, Transform, Load), a pattern driven by historical database limitations, typically used a dedicated external system to pull, transform, and clean data for a specific schema (like a Kimball star schema) before loading the final result into a data warehouse for business analytics.

In direct contrast, modern ELT (Extract, Load, Transform) reverses this pattern, leveraging the immense performance and storage of today’s data platforms (like warehouses, lakes, and lakehouses) to load raw data first and perform transformations using the platform’s own internal capabilities.

Ingesting data without a plan is a great recipe for a data swamp.

In current data architectures, the line between ETL and ELT is blurring, leading to the view that organizations should not standardize on one method but instead select the most appropriate technique for each individual data pipeline on a case-by-case basis.

7.3.1.3. SQL and Code-based Transformation Tools

SQL is a first-class citizen in big data ecosystems, and can be used to simplify data transformations with automatic optimization in SQL engines, whereas code-based tools like Spark offer more control but require manual optimization.

SQL is a declarative language to describe the desired data state, and despite its non-procedural nature, it can be used effectively to build complex data workflows and pipelines using common table expressions, scripts, or orchestration tools, sometimes more efficiently than procedural programming languages.

  • When determining whether to use SQL for batch transformations, consider avoiding it if the transformation is difficult, unreadable, or unmaintainable in SQL, or if reusable libraries are a necessity, as procedural languages are often better suited for such complex tasks.

  • Optimizing Spark and other code-heavy processing frameworks requires manual effort and adherence to best practices, including early filtering, reliance on core APIs, and careful UDF usage, contrasting with SQL’s automatic optimization.

7.3.1.4. Update patterns

Updating persisted data is a significant challenge in data engineering, particularly with evolving technologies, and the modern data lakehouse concept now integrates in-place updates, which are crucial for efficiency (avoiding full re-runs) and compliance with data deletion regulations like GDPR.

  • The truncate-and-reload update pattern is a method for refreshing data where the existing data in a table is completely erased and then replaced with a newly generated and transformed dataset.

  • The insert-only pattern is a method for maintaining a current data view by adding new, versioned records instead of altering existing ones, with the drawback of being slow when finding the latest record.

    A materialized view speeds up queries on insert-only tables by acting as a truncate-and-reload target table that stores the pre-computed current state of the data.
    For a robust audit trail, the insert-only pattern treats data as a sequential, append-only log where new records are added but never changed.

    ✦ In column-oriented OLAP databases, single-row inserts are an anti-pattern that causes high system load and fragmented data storage, leading to inefficient reads; the recommended solution is to load data in batches or micro-batches.

    ✦ The enhanced Lambda architecture, found in systems like BigQuery and Druid, is an exception that handles frequent inserts by hybridizing a streaming buffer with columnar storage, although deletes and in-place updates can still be expensive.
    In columnar databases, primary keys or uniqueness are not enforced by the system but are a logical construct that the data engineering team must manage with queries to define the current state of a table

  • Deletion is a critical function for regulatory compliance but is a more expensive operation than an insert in columnar systems and data lakes.

    A hard delete permanently removes a record from a database, while a soft delete marks the record as deleted.

    • Hard deletes are used to permanently remove data for performance, legal, or compliance reasons.

    • Soft deletes are used to filter records from query results without permanently deleting them.

      The insert-only pattern can also be used to create a new record with a deleted flag instead of altering the original to enable soft deletes within an immutable, append-only framework.

  • The upsert and merge patterns are update strategies that match records against a target table using a key, where upsert will either insert a new record or update an existing one, while the merge pattern also adds the ability to delete records.

    A merge operation is a superset of an upsert because, in addition to inserting and updating records, it also deletes records from the target table (the "old" data) that are absent from the source (the "new" data) with a full synchronization.

    • UPSERT = UPDATE + INSERT:

      • If a record from the source matches a record in the target (based on a key), it UPDATEs the target record.

      • If a record from the source does not match any record in the target, it INSERTs the new record.

    • MERGE = UPDATE + INSERT + DELETE:

      • It does everything an upsert does.

      • Additionally, if a record from the target table do not have a match in the source data, it DELETEs the target record.

    Merging data in batches causes incorrect deletions because records outside the current batch are misinterpreted by the MERGE operation as not matched by source. A common solution is to use a staging table to first assemble the complete source dataset, which enables a single, reliable merge operation and avoids the issues of direct batch processing.

    The pattern consists of the following steps:

    1. First, a temporary staging table is completely cleared of any existing data, often with a TRUNCATE command.

    2. Next, all batches of the source dataset are loaded into this staging table, typically using simple insert operations.

    3. Finally, after the staging table holds the complete source dataset, a single MERGE operation is executed to synchronize the data from the staging table to the final target table.
    The upsert and merge pattern was originally designed for row-based databases, where updates are a natural process that the database looks up the record in question and changes it in place. On the other hand, file-based systems don’t support in-place file updates, where the entire file must be rewritten even for single record changes, which led early big data and data lake adopters to reject updates in favor of insert-only patterns; however, columnar databases like Vertica have long supported in-place updates by abstracting the underlying Copy-on-Write complexity, a capability now common in major columnar cloud data warehouses.
7.3.1.5. Schema updates

In modern cloud data warehouse, a new option for semi-structured data, borrowing from document stores, is typically used to provide flexibility for schema updates by storing frequently accessed data in flattened fields alongside raw JSON.

Semi-structured data is a first-class citizen in data warehouses, opening new opportunities for data analysts and data scientists since data is no longer constrained to rows and columns.
7.3.1.6. Data Wrangling

Data wrangling is the process of transforming messy, malformed data into useful, clean data, typically through a batch transformation process, and has historically been a challenging task for data engineers.

  • Data wrangling tools, often presented as no-code solutions or IDEs for malformed data, aim to automate and simplify the process of cleaning and transforming data, freeing data engineers for more complex tasks and enabling analysts to assist with parsing.

  • Graphical data-wrangling tools provide visual interfaces for analyzing data, defining processing steps to fix issues, and executing these on scalable systems like Spark with iterative refinement, making them highly recommended for streamlining engineering tasks and widely available.

7.3.1.7. Example: Data transformation in Spark

In a typical data pipeline, Airflow orchestrates the initial ingestion of JSON data from multiple APIs into an S3 bucket, then triggers a Spark job to process this data. The Spark job reads the raw files, transforms them into a unified relational table (i.e., dataframe), and filters the results with a SQL query. Finally, Spark writes the processed data back to S3 as a compressed, Parquet-formatted Delta Lake table, after which Airflow marks the entire workflow as complete.

7.3.1.8. MapReduce

MapReduce is a foundational batch data transformation pattern from the big data era, first introduced by Google and widely popularized as the original processing engine for Hadoop. Although it is not commonly used directly by data engineers today, its core principles continue to influence the design of modern distributed systems, and is still valuable for grasping the fundamentals of large-scale data processing.

The classic MapReduce model works in distinct stages: map, shuffle, and reduce. Initially, map tasks run in parallel across a cluster, with each task reading and processing an individual block of data. Afterwards, the shuffle phase redistributes the intermediate results, ensuring all data for a specific key is moved to a single node. Finally, the reduce step aggregates this grouped data on each node to compute the final result. A defining characteristic of this paradigm is its rigidity and reliance on disk, as all data is written to and read from disk between tasks, with no intermediate state held in memory.

Modern data processing has moved into a post-MapReduce world with frameworks like Spark and BigQuery that prioritize in-memory processing. These systems still employ the concepts of map, shuffle, and reduce but relax the older constraints by using RAM as the primary tier for holding data. Data is only spilled to disk when it exceeds available memory, which dramatically speeds up performance. The adoption of this faster, more flexible in-memory approach has been driven largely by the cloud, which makes it cost-effective to lease the necessary memory for the duration of a processing job.

7.3.2. Materialized Views, Federation, and Query Virtualization

  • A view is a stored query used to simplify data access or enhance security, while a materialized view is a stored result set, pre-computed and saved to improve performance.

  • A federated query is a database feature that allows an OLAP database to select from an external data source, such as object storage or RDBMS.

    An external table is a database object that stores metadata about an external source (such as its location and file format) without ingesting the data itself, reading the data directly from that source only when the table is queried.

  • Data virtualization is a practice where a query engine like Trino or Presto, which doesn’t store data internally, is used to directly query and access data scattered across various external systems.

    • A key feature called query pushdown optimizes performance by moving parts of a query to the source database, which leverages that system’s processing power and reduces network traffic.

    • Data virtualization is a good solution for organizations with data stored across various sources, however, it must be used carefully because directly querying a live production system can negatively impact its performance.

    • Data virtualization can also be used as a component in data ingestion pipelines to pull data from a production system during off-peak hours and save it to a data lake, which protects the source system from direct analytical queries.

      A common strategy is to use it for scheduled data ingestion, pulling data during off-peak hours and saving it to a data lake.

    • In a modern data mesh architecture, data virtualization can serve as a critical access layer that expands the data lake, providing a unified way for different teams to share their data products across the company.

8. Data Serving

Data serving is the final stage of the data engineering lifecycle, where prepared data is delivered for downstream use cases such as analytics and BI, machine learning applications, and reverse ETL.

When serving data, several key factors must be considered to ensure it is effective and valuable. The most crucial consideration is trust; end-users must have confidence in the data’s quality, accuracy, and reliability, which is built and maintained through data validation, observability, and upholding Service Level Agreements (SLAs).

It is also vital to understand the use case and the user. Data should be action-oriented, and engineers should prioritize projects with the highest return on investment by understanding who will use the data and for what purpose. This leads to treating data as a data product, which involves understanding the user’s "job to be done" and creating solutions that meet their specific needs. A good data product is the result of understanding its users' goals, its specific audience (internal or external), and its expected return on investment, which in turn drives adoption and continuous improvement and feedback.

While the concept of self-service data is a popular aspiration, it is difficult to implement successfully and often fails in practice. The primary reason for failure is a mismatch between the self-service tools and the end-users' actual needs, as executives typically prefer pre-built, actionable dashboards while analysts already use more powerful tools like SQL.

Furthermore, data definitions and logic must be formally defined, documented, and consistently applied to ensure correctness, which prevents reliance on ambiguous institutional knowledge and can be managed effectively through a semantic layer. A data definition provides the specific, agreed-upon meaning of a term, such as what qualifies as a "customer," across all departments. Data logic, in turn, consists of the formal rules and formulas that use these definitions to derive key metrics, like "customer lifetime value."

Finally, an emerging consideration is the data mesh, an organizational structure that decentralizes data serving. In this model, domain-specific teams are responsible for both producing and consuming data, treating it as a product to be shared across the organization.

In the serving stage, data engineers interface with a wide range of stakeholders, including data analysts, data scientists, ML engineers, and business users, where the primary responsibility is to provide the highest-quality data products possible, not to interpret the data’s end uses. This support role requires managing feedback loops as data is rarely static, and establishing a clear separation of duties is crucial as a company matures to avoid unsustainable role overlap. In a data mesh architecture, these responsibilities are decentralized, requiring domain teams to effectively collaborate and manage their own data serving tasks.

8.1. Analytics

Analytics is a data-serving use case for discovering key insights, where success depends on first identifying the end goal to determine the right type of analytics to apply—such as business analytics for historical trends, operational analytics for real-time alerts, or embedded analytics for in-app dashboards.

8.1.1. Business analytics

Business analytics is the practice of using historical and current data to inform strategic, actionable decisions by combining statistical and trend analysis with domain expertise and human judgment. It is considered both an art and a science, primarily manifesting in dashboards, reports, and ad hoc analysis.

  • A dashboard is a business intelligence tool that provides a concise, visual summary of an organization’s performance against its most critical metrics, much like a car’s dashboard displays essential information for a driver. Tailored for decision-makers, dashboards can range from high-level executive overviews to more detailed views for specific departments, tracking KPIs and OKRs. Analysts are responsible for creating, maintaining, and updating these dashboards using BI platforms such as Tableau, Looker, or Power BI.

  • A report is a detailed analysis created to answer a specific business question, with the goal of using data to drive insights and action. Unlike a dashboard’s ongoing monitoring, a report is typically a one-time investigation into a particular issue, such as an analyst querying a data warehouse to determine the root cause of high product returns. The findings are then summarized and distributed to relevant stakeholders, often using the same BI tool where dashboards are hosted.

  • Ad hoc analysis is a one-time, exploratory investigation into a specific business question or issue, often serving as the starting point for what may later become a formal report or a new metric on a dashboard if the insights are significant. The tools for ad hoc analysis overlap with those for reports and dashboards but also frequently include more flexible options like Excel, Python or R notebooks, and direct SQL queries.

BI systems share the data processing workload with a source database, but the approach varies, like Tableau, pull data from the database to store and process it locally for interactive analysis. In contrast, modern BI systems like Looker use a query pushdown model, where they translate user interactions and predefined logic into SQL queries that are executed directly on the source database. To improve performance, both types of systems commonly use caching for frequently run queries.

A collaborative relationship between analysts and data engineers is crucial for effective business analytics; analysts provide vital feedback on data quality and request new datasets, while engineers are responsible for ingesting and preparing this data. This partnership creates a virtuous cycle, as demonstrated when engineers ingest supply-chain data that allows analysts to pinpoint a faulty supplier, leading to a direct business impact.

Data for analytics is typically served in batches from a data warehouse or lake at widely varying frequencies, but it is critical to remember that the initial ingestion frequency sets the speed limit for all downstream processes. Therefore, even if current use cases are batch-oriented, data from a streaming source should be ingested as a stream to preserve future real-time capabilities.

Finally, data engineers must consider the backend architecture, as some BI tools use an internal storage layer while others query the data warehouse directly. The direct-query approach leverages the power of the underlying database but requires careful management of cost, access control, and latency.

8.1.2. Operational Analytics

Operational analytics is distinguished from business analytics by its focus on using real-time data to take immediate action, whereas business analytics uses data to derive longer-term actionable insights. The key difference is the element of time; operational analytics requires up-to-the-second data to address problems as they happen.

The distinction between the two is blurring as streaming data becomes more common, pushing data products toward a streaming-first future. This trend underscores the principle that the value of real-time data is contingent on taking correct action, without which it is merely a distraction.

Real-time application monitoring is a primary example of operational analytics, enabling software engineering teams to track key performance metrics like requests per second or database I/O on a live dashboard, which allows for immediate, automated actions, such as triggering server scaling events when load increases or sending alerts via text, chat, or email when critical thresholds are breached.

8.1.3. Embedded Analytics

Embedded analytics are external-facing dashboards and metrics integrated directly into an application for the end user that, in contrast to the internal focused business and operational analytics, provide users with data about their own interactions to empower better, often real-time, decisions.

For instance, a smart thermostat app empowers users by showing real-time power consumption to help them create more energy-efficient schedules, while an e-commerce platform might provide sellers with a live dashboard of sales and inventory to inform timely customer deals. In both cases, the application uses embedded analytics to provide data that allows the end user to make immediate, data-driven decisions.

Data engineers supporting embedded analytics must provide backend databases that solve three key performance challenges: low data latency, fast query performance, and high concurrency.

8.2. Machine Learning

Machine learning (ML), a field of artificial intelligence where computer systems learn from data to make predictions and decisions, relies on a collaborative data serving process where data engineers prepare and deliver tailored data for model training and execution, involving transforming raw data into numerical features through featurization, such as encoding categorical data and creating embeddings, and implementing and maintaining robust data pipelines for both batch and streaming delivery to feed ML models, often in collaboration with ML engineers.

While a data engineer doesn’t need to have a deep understanding of ML, a foundational knowledge of its core principles is essential for effectively supporting the machine learning lifecycle. This includes understanding fundamental concepts such as the differences between supervised and unsupervised learning, classification, and regression, and knowing when to use classical algorithms versus deep learning. Proficiency in data-centric tasks like data wrangling, feature engineering, and handling time-series data is also crucial. Furthermore, a data engineer should grasp the operational aspects of ML, such as the distinctions between batch and online learning, the implications of different hardware choices (CPU vs. GPU), the role of technologies like feature stores, and the importance of data quality to prevent issues like data cascades.

9. Data Serving for Analytics and ML

Data engineers empower analytics and machine learning by serving data through a comprehensive suite of methods, including traditional file exchanges and databases, modern streaming and federated query systems, as well as advanced options like data sharing platforms, semantic layers, and direct notebook integration.

9.1. File Exchange

File exchange is a common method for serving structured, semi-structured, and unstructured data to consumers. The way files are served depends on factors like the use case, the consumer’s data handling processes, file size, and data type. Simple methods like emailing files are problematic due to a lack of version control and access revocation, making collaboration platforms like Google Docs or Microsoft 365 preferable for maintaining a single, consistent version of a file. For larger-scale needs, file exchange evolves into using object storage or data lakes. However, at that scale, it is often considered a more streamlined process akin to data sharing rather than a simple ad-hoc file exchange.

9.2. Databases

Databases, particularly OLAP systems like data warehouses and data lakes, are a critical layer for serving data in analytics and ML. The process involves querying the database and consuming the results, for instance by exporting them to a CSV file or analyzing them in a notebook. Serving data from a database offers significant benefits, including the order and structure imposed by schemas, the ability to implement fine-grained access controls at the table, column, and row levels, and high performance for computationally intensive queries and high concurrency. For example, in a machine learning workflow, a data scientist might connect to a database to extract data, perform feature engineering and selection, and then feed the resulting dataset into an offline model for training and generating predictions.

9.3. Streaming Systems

Streaming systems are increasingly vital for serving data in analytics and ML, representing a paradigm shift from traditional queries to continuously emitted metrics. A key development in this area is the rise of operational analytics databases, which combine the features of OLAP databases and stream-processing systems, which allows queries to run on a vast range of data, from historical to the most current, up-to-the-second information.

9.4. Query Federation

Query federation is a pattern that allows a single query to pull data from multiple diverse sources—like data lakes, databases, and data warehouses—without first centralizing the data. This approach offers significant flexibility for ad-hoc exploratory analysis and is ideal for situations where data access needs to be tightly controlled, providing secure, read-only access that is beneficial for compliance.

However, this method presents challenges, primarily the risk of federated queries consuming excessive resources on live production systems. It serves as a practical way to blend data and determine if the performance is sufficient for ongoing needs or if a more permanent solution, like centralizing the data into an OLAP system via ETL pipelines, is required.

9.5. Data Sharing

Data sharing is a serving model where data is exchanged between different organizations or business units through massively multitenant cloud storage systems like Snowflake, Redshift, and BigQuery. In this pattern, the responsibility for running queries shifts from the data engineers to the data consumers (analysts and data scientists). This reframes the primary challenge of data serving into one of managing security and access control, making it a compelling and increasingly core feature of major data platforms for sharing data safely and securely.

9.6. Semantic and Metrics Layers

A semantic or metrics layer is a tool that standardizes business logic to ensure that queries produce accurate and consistent analytics, built on the principle that even the most powerful query engines will quickly return bad results when fed poor-quality queries.

These layers solve this problem by providing a central place to define and maintain key business metrics. Tools like Looker (with LookML) or dbt (Data Build Tool) allow for the creation of reusable, complex business logic. When a user requests a metric, the tool generates the correct SQL query based on this standardized definition, which prevents the inconsistencies and repetition found in traditional ETL scripts.

  • Looker, using its language LookML, operates primarily at the serving and reporting layer. It defines business logic virtually and generates complex SQL queries on the fly when a user interacts with a report or dashboard.

  • dbt, in contrast, operates exclusively in the transformation layer. It serves as a robust pipeline orchestration tool for analytics engineers to build and materialize data models directly in the warehouse, which BI tools then query.

By ensuring that everyone in an organization uses the same underlying calculations for the same business concepts, these tools directly address the critical question, "Are these numbers correct?" and build trust in the data.

9.7. Notebooks

Serving data to notebooks, the primary tool for data scientists, begins with establishing programmatic connections to sources like databases, data lakes, or APIs. A key role for the data engineer is to assist data scientists in discovering the correct data and ensuring they have the proper permissions to access it.

A common workflow for data scientists is to load data into a pandas DataFrame on a local machine, which inevitably fails when the dataset’s size exceeds the available memory. The solution is to guide data scientists off their laptops and onto scalable cloud infrastructure. This transition typically follows a path from cloud-hosted notebooks to distributed execution systems (like Dask, Ray, or Spark) and eventually to fully managed ML platforms such as SageMaker, Vertex AI, or Azure ML. Data and ML engineers are crucial in leading this move by setting up the infrastructure, managing environments, and training scientists on these more powerful tools.

Finally, notebooks can even be used in production to accelerate deployment, an approach with significant trade-offs. While it allows data scientists to move faster, it is often considered a substandard production practice. The alternative, having engineers rewrite notebooks for production, creates a bottleneck. A hybrid approach is often ideal, where notebooks are used for light production tasks and a full, robust productionization process is reserved for high-value projects.

10. Reverse ETL

Reverse ETL is the process of serving data by taking processed information from an analytical system, like a data warehouse, and loading it back into an operational source system, such as a CRM or marketing platform. The primary goal is to reduce friction for end-users by delivering valuable data directly into the tools they use for their daily work. For example, instead of providing a sales team with a separate dashboard, reverse ETL would load machine learning-generated lead scores directly into the customer profiles within their CRM.

While the name "reverse ETL" is not perfectly descriptive, the practice of moving data from OLAP systems back into source systems is an increasingly important and formalized data engineering responsibility. Although custom solutions can be built, it is often better to use one of the many available open-source or commercial tools, keeping in mind that the vendor landscape is new and changing rapidly.

A significant word of caution is that reverse ETL inherently creates feedback loops. If an error exists in the processing logic (e.g., an ad bidding model), feeding the flawed output back into the source system can amplify the error, potentially leading to major negative consequences like wasting massive amounts of money. Therefore, it is critical to implement robust monitoring and guardrails when using this serving pattern.

Appendix A: Serialization and Compression

A.1. Serialization Formats

Serialization, the process of converting data for storage or transmission, is a critical foundation of data engineering where the choice of format has massive performance implications. The primary decision lies between row-oriented formats (like JSON and Avro), which excel at handling individual records, and columnar formats (like Parquet), which are highly optimized for large-scale analytical queries through efficient I/O and compression.

Modern innovations are advancing the field even further. Apache Arrow provides a standard for in-memory columnar data to eliminate serialization overhead between processes, while hybrid table formats like Apache Iceberg and Hudi act as a management layer on top of these formats to provide reliable, transactional capabilities and features like time travel directly on the data lake.

A.1.1. Row-Based Serialization

Row-based serialization formats, such as the archetypal CSV, organize data by row. For semistructured data (data objects that support nesting and schema variation), row-oriented serialization entails storing each object as a unit.

  • CSV is a slow and error-prone "nonstandard standard" due to its many variations in conventions, such as different delimiters and quoting rules, which makes it unsuitable for data pipelines. When using CSV exchanging data with external systems or for data archival, it is critical to provide a complete technical description of the specific format configuration to ensure the data remains usable in the future.

  • Extensible Markup Language (XML) is a legacy format that is generally slow to serialize and deserialize in data engineering applications. Although largely replaced by JSON for plain-text object serialization, data engineers are still often required to use XML when interacting with legacy systems.

  • JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) has become the modern standard for data exchange over APIs and is a popular format for data storage. Its widespread native support in major databases, from document stores to cloud data warehouses, simplifies the process of moving data between applications and analytical systems.

  • JSONL (JSON Lines) is a specialized format that stores bulk semistructured data by delimiting each JSON object with a line break, making it highly effective for initial data ingestion. For subsequent pipeline stages, however, JSONL should be converted into a more performant columnar format to optimize for transformation and serving.

  • Avro is a row-oriented data format designed for RPCs and data serialization, which encodes data into a compact binary format while defining the schema separately in JSON. It is a popular format within the Hadoop ecosystem and is also supported by many cloud data tools.

A.1.2. Columnar Serialization

Columnar serialization organizes data by storing each column in its own set of files, a fundamental pivot from row-oriented formats, which is highly optimized for analytical workloads because queries need to scan only the necessary columns instead of entire rows, and grouping similar data together enables highly efficient compression, such as tokenization for repeated values and standard algorithms for redundant data, which maximizes storage and network resources.

Columnar formats are inefficient for record-level operations because accessing a single record requires reconstruction from multiple files, and updating a field is extremely costly due to the need to decompress and rewrite entire column segments, which makes them ill-suited for transactional (OLTP) workloads that rely on more efficient row-oriented storage.

  • Parquet is a columnar format designed for high performance in data lakes. It improves on formats like CSV by including schema information and native support for nested data. Crucially, Parquet is also highly portable, avoiding the significant performance penalties that proprietary warehouse formats incur when used with external data lake tools like Spark. To maximize efficiency, Parquet is almost always used with a compression codec, such as the speed-optimized Snappy algorithm.

  • Optimized Row Columnar (ORC) is a columnar storage format similar to Parquet, which was historically popular for its use with Apache Hive. Although still widely used, ORC is now generally less common than Parquet and has more limited support across the modern cloud data ecosystem. This support gap is illustrated by tools like Snowflake and BigQuery, which can import data from ORC files but, unlike with Parquet, cannot export data back into the ORC format.

  • Apache Arrow is an in-memory, language-agnostic columnar format designed to eliminate the significant performance overhead of traditional serialization and deserialization. It achieves this by providing a single, standardized binary format that can be used for high-performance data processing in memory, transfer over the network, and long-term storage, thus avoiding costly data conversion steps.

    To address the challenge of different programming languages having unique memory layouts, the Arrow project provides libraries that allow diverse languages like Java, Python, and C++ to work on the same data in memory with zero-copy efficiency. This powerful interoperability has led to its rapid adoption in major frameworks like Apache Spark and has inspired new, Arrow-native data platforms such as Dremio.

A.1.3. Hybrid Serialization

Hybrid serialization refers to technologies, such as Apache Hudi and Apache Iceberg, that either combine multiple serialization techniques or integrate a serialization format with an additional abstraction layer for tasks like schema management.

  • Apache Hudi (Hadoop Update Delete Incremental) is a table management technology that enables both high-performance analytical queries and atomic, transactional updates on the same table. It achieves this with a hybrid approach, storing the bulk of the data in a columnar format for fast analytics while ingesting new updates from streams (like CDC) into a row-oriented format for write efficiency. Queries provide a real-time view by combining data from both formats, and a periodic repacking process merges the row-based updates into the columnar store to maintain long-term query performance.

  • Like Hudi, Apache Iceberg is a table management technology that tracks the individual files making up a data lake table, and through this snapshot-tracking ability, it enables key features such as table time travel (the ability to query the table as it existed at a specific point in the past), robust schema evolution, and the management of petabyte-scale tables.

A.2. Compression

Compression algorithms reduce data size by identifying and removing redundancy and repetition, then re-encoding the data into a more compact format. The process is reversed during decompression to perfectly reconstruct the original data. A simple analogy is replacing frequently used words in a text with shorter tokens; sophisticated algorithms use advanced mathematical techniques to achieve much higher compression ratios, often reaching 10:1 for text.

Lossless compression restores a bit-for-bit exact copy of the original data upon decompression, which is critical for analytics where data fidelity must be perfect. In contrast, lossy compression, used for audio, images, and video, recovers a version that looks or sounds like the original but is not an exact copy, as it prioritizes reducing file size over perfect data integrity.

Traditional compression algorithms like gzip and bzip2 excel at achieving high compression ratios, especially for text-based formats such as JSON and CSV. In contrast, a newer generation of algorithms, including Snappy, Zstandard, and LZ4, prioritizes high-speed performance and CPU efficiency over achieving the maximum possible compression. These faster algorithms are commonly used in data lakes and columnar databases where quick query performance is more critical than minimizing storage size.

xz is a modern compression format that uses the LZMA2 algorithm, known for achieving a very high compression ratio, that provides superior compression (smaller files) at the cost of being much slower and more resource-intensive, making it ideal for final archives or software distribution. In contrast, gzip is significantly faster and more efficient, making it the standard for on-the-fly compression (such as web content before transmission) where speed is more critical than achieving the absolute minimum file size.

A .zip file is both an archival format that bundles files together and a compression format that reduces their size (typically using the same DEFLATE algorithm as gzip). Because a .zip file’s contents are already compressed, it is not a good target for further compression. Attempting to compress a zip file will yield almost no size reduction and can sometimes even make it slightly larger.

The effectiveness of compression hinges on the data’s redundancy, making text-based data such as logs, JSON, and CSV files excellent targets due to their highly repetitive nature. Similarly, raw uncompressed binary formats like bitmap images are also good candidates. However, it is inefficient to compress data that is already in a compressed format, as this provides little to no additional size reduction. This category of poor targets includes common media files like JPEG and MP3, archive files like ZIP, and application packages like JAR and DLL files, all of which contain internal compression or have low redundancy, making them unsuitable for further compression.

Streaming compression works by breaking the continuous data flow into manageable chunks or blocks, as the entire stream is not available at once. To effectively find patterns, algorithms use a sliding window that maintains a buffer of the most recent data to use as a dictionary for compressing the current chunk. Each compressed chunk is then wrapped in a self-contained frame that includes metadata, such as its size and a checksum. This creates a continuous stream of independent frames, allowing a decompressor on the receiving end to read and decompress each piece individually to reconstruct the original data flow.

References

  • [1] Joe Reis, Matt Housley Fundamentals of Data Engineering: Plan and Build Robust Data Systems, 1st Edition, O’Reilly Media, July 26, 2022
